chunks: From him, from Ahmad ibn al-Hasan ibn Ali, from Amr ibn Sa'id, from Musaddiq ibn Sadah, from 'Ammar, from Abu Abdillah (peace be upon him)

From a man: Is it permissible for him to advance gold dinars for such and such dirhams to a known term? He said: 'Yes, there is no harm.' And from a man: Is it permissible for him to buy gold dinars on credit (nasi'ah)? He said: 'Yes, only gold and other than it are equal in buying and selling.'

Muhammad ibn al-Hasan said: The resolution in these narrations is that they do not contradict what we previously stated, that the sale of gold for silver on credit with an increase is not permissible, because those narrations are numerous and these are only four, the main one of which is 'Ammar ibn Musa al-Sabati, who is a single narrator (fard), and a group of narrators have weakened him, saying that what he narrates alone is not acted upon because he was 'fatahi' (lacking in precision), but we do not attack him in this way, because even if he is so, he is trustworthy in narration and not attacked in it. As for the report of Zurarah, the path to it is Ali ibn Hadeed, who is very weak and reliance is not placed on what he narrates alone. These narrations can bear an interpretation, which is that his saying 'on credit' is a description of the dinars, not a condition of the sale, so the summary of the matter is that whoever has on credit (debt) gold dinars from another, it is permissible for him to sell them to him immediately for dirhams at the current price or more than that, and take the price immediately. And we will mention after this what indicates the permissibility of that, if God wills.

As for what was narrated: Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Yahya, from Muhammad ibn Isa, from al-Fadl ibn Kathir, from Muhammad ibn Amr, who said: I wrote to Abu al-Hasan al-Rida (peace be upon him) that a woman from our people bequeathed that we deliver to you thirty dinars, and they were with me, and I did not have them with me, so I went to some of the money-changers and said: Advance me dinars on condition that I give you the price of each dinar as twenty-six dirhams, so I took from him ten dinars for two hundred and sixty dirhams, and I have sent them to you. He wrote back (peace be upon him): 'The dinars have reached me.'

So this report contains no more than the narration of the state of what he did by advancing dirhams for dinars and sending them to al-Rida (peace be upon him) for a transfer that had occurred to him, and that he accepted it from him, and it does not contain that he asked him about the permissibility of that so he validated it and permitted it for him. And if that is not in it, then it does not contradict what we previously stated, and that which indicates what we previously stated is what was narrated.
ai.seo_question: Is it permissible to sell gold for silver on credit with an increase in Shia fiqh?
ai.summary: Shaykh al-Tusi analyzes the apparent contradiction between narrations permitting the sale of gold for silver on credit with an increase and the general prohibition of *nasi'ah* (delay) in unequal exchanges. He resolves this by distinguishing between the debt itself being described as credit versus the sale transaction being deferred, and notes the reliance on specific narrators like Ammar ibn Musa and the acceptance of the Imam's silent approval (*sukut*) in the case of the woman's will.
